https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/nato-figh.text: Charlie Bradley Updated Sun, September 13, 2026 at 12:47 PM UTC 0 NATO fighter jets (Image: Getty) NATO fighter jets have been scrambled amid reports that a Russian drone was headed for Lithuania, but this was later confirmed to be a flock of birds. Flights were suspended at Vilnius Airport in the country's capital, and the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre issued a yellow alert for possible drone hazard in Vilnius, Trakai, and Elektrenai districts. The air alert has since been lifted by authorities. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Center, said after the alert: "There is no threat, people can calm down. (...) In principle, the threat level has been eliminated." According to the Lithuanian Armed Forces, radars near Varna detected an object moving towards the Kaliningrad region. Authorities later confirmed: "Fighter jets carrying out a NATO air policing mission were deployed to inspect the object. They determined that the radar signals were a flock of birds." The Lithuanian military said earlier this week that drones aimed at Ukraine have landed in Lithuanian territory. Commander of the Armed Forces of Lithuania General Raimundas Vaikšnoras confirmed that Russian "Gerbera" drones were originally fired at Ukrainian cities before landing in Lithuania. Vilnius Airport (Image: Getty) Russia has issued numerous threats to Lithuania as the country continues to boost its defences amid fears it could be attacked by Moscow's forces. Just this week, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev suggested wiping Lithuania "off the map." He said: "No one will come to their defence. Even if the place is reduced to scorched earth, no other country will go to war for them. And the well-known Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty - it will not be invoked, everyone recognises that. Because if it is invoked, it will be a global catastrophe, a planetary one. They are not fools. https://www.theargus.co.uk/news/26708296.text: Crime West Sussex Crime gang jailed for more than 100 years for drugs plot Crime West Sussex By Joseph Blakely Reporter Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A crime gang who attempted to smuggle half a tonne of cocaine into Sussex has been sentenced to more than 100 years in prison. The 12 members of the organised crime group were jailed for plotting to bring 500kg of cocaine, worth an estimated £40 million, into the UK. The gang’s plot was foiled on August 19, 2024, when National Crime Agency officers intercepted the group as they landed 16 bales of cocaine on Medmerry Beach near Selsey. It is believed the drugs had been dropped into the sea a few days earlier by a crew aboard a container ship about 40 nautical miles south of the Needles, to the west of the Isle of Wight. The cocaine, with a purity of around 85 per cent, was packaged in waterproof bundles equipped with GPS trackers. The cocaine was pulled from the sea packaged in waterproof bales (Image: National Crime Agency) All 12 members were sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on November 5 and 6. The ringleaders were identified as Daniel Jamieson, 41, and Sam Brown, 33. Jamieson, of Heath Road, Ramsden Heath, Essex, was sentenced to 22 years in prison after being found guilty of conspiring to smuggle cocaine. He posed as a legitimate businessman and, under a false identity, acquired a maritime business and the inflatable boat used to recover the drugs. Brown, of Wykeham Street, Kirkdale, Liverpool, admitted the same charge and was jailed for 16 years and six months. Originally from Essex, Brown was said to have recruited others to join the conspiracy, including his friend Harry Kennedy, 38, who lived on the same street in Liverpool. Kennedy, who became involved the day before the drugs were landed, pleaded guilty to the same charge and was sentenced to nine years. Messages recovered during the investigation revealed that Brown and Kennedy were also involved in separate drug supply activities. Carl Powner, 62, of Park Road, Stoke-on-Trent, was sentenced to 13 years. He played a key role in the operation, recruiting drivers, sourcing equipment, and sailing out to recover the cocaine. Powner originally fled abroad but was arrested in Romania in May and extradited to the UK. He retrieved the drugs from the sea alongside Adil Nolan, 40, of Maureen Walk, Fazakerley, Liverpool, Nolan was sentenced to 11 years and three months after admitting conspiracy to smuggle cocaine. Oil rig worker David Paterson, 49, of Viking Way, Peterhead, near Aberdeen, had attempted an earlier retrieval of the drugs on August 17, but failed due to malfunctioning trackers. Paterson was convicted of conspiracy to smuggle cocaine and sentenced to 14 years. Lewis Watts, 37, of Toronto Road, Tilbury, Essex, was described as Jamieson’s "right-hand man," responsible for logistics and communication. He was in charge of a pre-paid credit card set up to fund the conspiracy, sourced equipment and acted as a go-between for conspirators in real life and online. He was sentenced to 14 years after being found guilty at trial of conspiracy to smuggle cocaine. Collectively the drugs weighed half a tonne and were worth an estimated £40 million (Image: National Crime Agency) A further five individuals, involved in the landing operation on Medmerry Beach, were convicted of assisting an organised crime group. Charlotte Blenman, 34, of Shelley Road East, Boscombe, Bournemouth, received a 20-month sentence suspended for two years. Roy Harmer, 46, of Chine Road, Bournemouth; Neil Pinchbeck, 43, of Pearce Road, Poole; Thomas Stewart, 40, of Carpenter Close, Peterborough; and Ricky Platt, 49, of Westby Road, Boscombe, each received 20-month prison sentences. Read more Traveller wins permission to keep mobile home after battle with council Fire-damaged convent site goes up for auction amid major housing plans Plans for hundreds of homes on edge of city withdrawn Jules Harriman, senior investigating officer at the NCA, said: "The main players from this conspiracy are facing very long periods behind bars. "Had their smuggling attempt worked, these toxic drugs would have brought misery and violence to many communities around the country. "The crime group responsible for supplying these offenders has lost their drugs and massive profits that can no longer be ploughed back into further offending. "Working with partners such as Border Force, the NCA will continue to do all it can to protect the public from the threat of Class A drugs." The NCA thanked Merseyside Police, West Mercia Police, Hampshire Police, and Sussex Police for their support during the investigation.
